paragraphs: Learning-augmented algorithms make decisions with help from predictions that may be wrong. Much of the existing work assumes these predictions arrive as part of the input, without restricting how much advice is available. This paper changes that setup by giving the algorithm a limited number of predictions that it can request during execution.

That restriction makes obtaining advice part of the decision problem itself. The algorithm must address both when a prediction is worth requesting and how to use the information it receives. Because requests can occur during execution, the framework explicitly brings the timing of advice into the study, alongside the possibility that advice is inaccurate.

The authors examine this setting through three classical problems: ski rental, the secretary problem, and non-clairvoyant job scheduling. These provide distinct contexts for studying decisions under limited advice. The contribution described in the abstract is the budget-constrained formulation and its investigation across these problems, centering attention on prediction access as a resource that algorithms must manage.
neurips-2023-advice-querying-under-budge.tldr: The paper studies when online algorithms should request potentially incorrect predictions when only a limited number of requests is available.

paragraphs: Differentially private training must balance privacy protection, model usefulness, and computation. Matrix factorization mechanisms have improved this balance in several settings, but they have remained difficult to apply in some cases or less competitive at tighter privacy budgets. This paper develops a common construction intended to cover both centralized and federated training.

The key is to use banded, lower-triangular matrices, whose nonzero entries occupy a limited number of diagonal bands. In cross-device federated learning, this structure supports devices participating multiple times under a more relaxed participation arrangement. The authors report a production deployment demonstrating that the arrangement can fit practical federated learning infrastructure.

For centralized training, the authors prove that these banded mechanisms obtain the same privacy amplification results as DP-SGD. They show how the framework can incorporate prior leading approaches across privacy budgets, allowing it to at least match DP-SGD and often improve on it. The significance is a more unified approach to private training whose structure addresses both privacy analysis and deployment constraints.
neurips-2023-amplified-banded-matrix-fac.tldr: Banded matrix factorizations unify private training approaches while supporting practical federated participation and DP-SGD-style privacy amplification.

paragraphs: Anchor Data Augmentation addresses regression, where a model predicts numerical values, with particular attention to nonlinear models that have many parameters. The paper asks how to create additional training examples that support more robust predictions. Its starting point is Anchor regression, a distributionally robust method connected to the causality literature.

The proposed algorithm turns the sample modifications used in Anchor regression into a data augmentation procedure. It uses several replicas of modified samples to expand the training set. This gives the robustness-oriented construction a second role: it becomes a way to supply additional examples for training regression models, including neural networks.

The authors apply the method to both linear and nonlinear regression problems and report performance competitive with leading C-Mixup approaches. That comparison supports Anchor Data Augmentation as another viable approach to regression augmentation, without establishing that it always performs better. Its central contribution is the connection between a distributionally robust regression method and the practical task of generating more training data.
neurips-2023-anchor-data-augmentation-d6.tldr: Anchor Data Augmentation adapts a distributionally robust regression method to generate training examples and achieves performance competitive with C-Mixup.

paragraphs: A language model's input limit restricts how much earlier material it can use at once. LongMem addresses this by storing past context in a separate memory and training the model to retrieve and use it. The goal is to make information from a long history available beyond the model's immediate input.

The architecture separates memory encoding from memory reading. The original language model remains frozen and encodes memories, while an adaptive residual side-network learns retrieval and reading. This separation lets stored contexts be cached and updated without the memory staleness problem described by the authors. Memory-augmented adaptation training teaches the system to use the stored material.

The retrieval module is designed for a memory bank without a fixed context-length ceiling, and the paper describes memory extending to 65,000 tokens. That memory can hold many demonstration examples for in-context learning. Experiments outperform strong long-context models on ChapterBreak and improve memory-augmented in-context learning, supporting the usefulness of retrieving long histories for the evaluated tasks.
neurips-2023-augmenting-language-models-.tldr: LongMem combines a frozen language model with an adaptive memory-reading network to use long histories and improve evaluated long-context tasks.

paragraphs: Machine learning research on weather and climate can be difficult to reproduce when datasets, training procedures, and evaluations differ or are incompletely specified. ClimateLearn addresses this infrastructure problem with an open-source PyTorch library. Its purpose is to make training and evaluating models for weather and climate tasks more accessible and consistent.

The library provides connected pipelines for processing datasets, implementing deep learning models, and assessing results quantitatively and qualitatively. Supported examples include ERA5, CMIP6, and PRISM data, together with model families such as Transformers and ResNets. Bringing these components together helps researchers work within a shared framework for standard modeling tasks.

The authors demonstrate the library through forecasting and downscaling experiments. They also provide documentation, contribution guidance, and quickstart tutorials to support broader participation. The paper's main contribution is this research platform and its demonstrated capabilities: it connects weather and climate modeling workflows with modern machine learning tools while directly addressing the reproducibility problems motivating the work.
neurips-2023-climatelearn-benchmarking-m.tldr: ClimateLearn provides shared data, modeling, and evaluation pipelines to support reproducible machine learning research on weather and climate.

paragraphs: This paper studies clients learning which actions to choose while communicating over a randomly changing network. The same action can have different reward distributions for different clients, so collaboration must account for heterogeneous information. Rewards are independent over time, and the analysis covers both sub-Gaussian and sub-exponential reward environments.

The framework combines methods for generating random communication graphs with averaging-based consensus, a new weighting technique, and upper confidence bound action selection. Its algorithms explicitly account for graph randomness and remove the conventional doubly stochasticity assumption. At initialization, they require only knowledge of the number of clients.

The authors establish high-probability bounds on the system's overall regret, which measures the cost of learning through imperfect choices. Instance-dependent bounds grow logarithmically with time and are optimal in the studied setting. An instance-free bound grows as the square root of time times a logarithmic factor and is nearly optimal. These guarantees include communication randomness, extending beyond expected-regret analyses with more restrictive assumptions.
neurips-2023-decentralized-randomly-dist.tldr: A decentralized bandit framework coordinates clients with different rewards over random networks and provides high-probability regret guarantees.

paragraphs: In cooperative multi-agent reinforcement learning, agents receive a shared team reward even when their experiences and strategies differ. That makes it difficult to identify which individual experiences deserve attention during training. DIFFER addresses this problem by deriving individual rewards that can guide the replay of previously collected experiences.

The derivation requires network gradients to remain invariant and expresses that requirement as a partial differential equation. Solving it produces closed-form individual reward functions. These rewards allow individual temporal-difference errors to be computed, giving a signal of each experience's importance for learning and a basis for deciding how to use it in training.

The framework is equivalent to the original learning setup when individual experiences are homogeneous. When experiences differ, it adapts replay to improve efficiency and fairness across those experiences. Experiments on popular benchmarks report significant improvements in both learning efficiency and fairness. The contribution connects the mathematical decomposition of team rewards to a concrete training decision: which individual experiences the learning system revisits.
neurips-2023-differ-decomposing-individu.tldr: DIFFER derives individual rewards from shared team rewards to guide fairer and more efficient experience replay in cooperative multi-agent learning.

paragraphs: Super-resolution models often learn from images degraded by a predetermined process, such as a particular downsampling method. Real test images may instead contain different blur, noise, or compression effects, reducing reconstruction quality. SRTTA addresses this mismatch by adapting a super-resolution model at test time to different or unknown degradation types.

A pretrained degradation classifier first predicts the test image's degradation type. The framework then applies a second-order degradation scheme to construct paired data from that image. Feature-level reconstruction learning links the initial test image with its further-degraded counterparts, supplying an adaptation signal intended to help the model produce plausible high-resolution outputs.

This approach targets the time cost of methods that estimate degradation and train an image-specific model, while considering a broader range of corruption types. Experiments use synthesized corrupted DIV2K datasets with eight degradations and several real-world datasets. The authors report improved results over existing methods with satisfactory speed, supporting the framework's usefulness for the tested changes in image degradation.
neurips-2023-efficient-test-time-adaptat.tldr: SRTTA adapts super-resolution models using further-degraded versions of each test image, improving results across tested corruptions with satisfactory speed.

paragraphs: Advanced graph neural networks often use operations beyond standard message passing, which can complicate implementation. This paper investigates how transforming the graph itself can let ordinary message passing simulate many such networks without losing expressivity. The central question is whether a different graph representation can preserve what a more specialized network can distinguish.

The authors separate two kinds of simulation. Weak simulation matches expressivity after several message-passing steps, whereas strong simulation does so after every step. They provide a direct way to translate common operations from nonstandard graph networks into graph transformations supporting one of these forms of simulation.

This matters practically because the resulting models can use message-passing operations already available in standard libraries, reducing implementation difficulties and enabling better code optimization. On molecular benchmark datasets, message passing over transformed graphs achieves competitive predictive performance and sometimes exceeds the original networks. Those experiments complement the expressivity analysis by showing that the transformed implementations can also work well in evaluated prediction tasks.
neurips-2023-expressivity-preserving-gnn.tldr: Graph transformations let standard message passing simulate many advanced graph neural networks while preserving their expressivity.

paragraphs: Weight decay helps prevent overfitting, but its value can also substantially affect convergence in federated learning. The paper identifies a tension: regularizing local models can shift optimization away from the global objective. Multiple local updates and differences between clients' data amplify this effect, making weight decay an important part of federated optimization.

FedNAR is a plug-in designed for integration with existing federated learning algorithms. It controls update magnitudes by jointly clipping the gradient and weight decay. This treats the two contributions together when regulating a local update. The authors also provide a theoretical analysis of the resulting convergence rate.

Experiments on vision and language datasets, using different underlying federated optimizers, consistently show faster convergence and higher accuracy when FedNAR is added. The method also remains resilient across tested hyperparameter configurations and can adjust weight decay when its initial value is poorly chosen. These findings suggest that controlling regularization within the update process can improve both optimization and tolerance to imperfect parameter choices.
neurips-2023-fednar-federated-optimizati.tldr: FedNAR jointly regulates gradients and weight decay to improve federated learning convergence, accuracy, and resilience to imperfect hyperparameter choices.

paragraphs: Recording many neurons across brain regions creates a need to distinguish different ways those regions represent information. Partial information decomposition separates information that is unique to a source, shared redundantly, or available through sources jointly. Computing these quantities and estimating them reliably from limited data are both challenging.

The paper introduces an efficient method for computing and estimating a particular decomposition for multivariate Gaussian distributions. Empirical tests show an intuitive additivity property and recovery of known answers in canonical examples, including high-dimensional cases. The authors also propose and evaluate a correction for bias caused by having a finite number of samples.

Applied to mouse brain recordings, the method identifies greater redundancy between visual areas when a stimulus matters for behavior. This finding describes how the measured information relationship changes with behavioral relevance. Together, the computational method, empirical validation, and bias correction make the Gaussian decomposition more usable for studying information across brain regions under the distributional setting considered.
neurips-2023-gaussian-partial-informatio.tldr: An efficient Gaussian information decomposition with finite-sample bias correction reveals increased redundancy between mouse visual areas for behaviorally relevant stimuli.

paragraphs: This paper examines how much instruction tuning with open resources improves language models across a broad range of abilities. The authors train models ranging from 6.7 billion to 65 billion parameters using 12 instruction datasets. Their evaluations cover factual knowledge, reasoning, multilingual abilities, coding, safety, and open-ended instruction following.

The study combines automatic, model-based, and human-based assessment and introduces the Tülu model suite, trained on a mixture of high-quality open resources. Different datasets strengthen different skills, and no dataset or mixture performs best everywhere. Preference-based evaluations by models and humans also miss capability differences that benchmark evaluations reveal.

Taking the best model separately for each evaluation, the reported average reaches 87% of ChatGPT performance and 73% of GPT-4 performance. These figures do not describe one model winning across all tasks. The results support broader evaluation and further investment in base models and training data. Released models, code, data, and evaluation tools make the study's approach available for subsequent research.
neurips-2023-how-far-can-camels-go-explo.tldr: A broad study of open instruction tuning finds skill-specific gains, persistent performance gaps, and capability differences that preference evaluations can miss.

paragraphs: Image-language pretraining produces useful image representations, but adapting them to video with little supervision remains challenging. This paper adapts an image CLIP model through self-supervised learning tied to language. It modifies the backbone to model time and trains it through self-distillation, with objectives expressed in a space of action concepts.

That concept space is constructed from language-encoder features for relevant textual prompts. A large language model generates prompts describing actions and their attributes. The resulting language representations give the video training process a way to express relationships between actions and their characteristics, bringing action-oriented information into adaptation.

The authors introduce concept distillation and concept alignment objectives. These aim to retain the original representations' generality while enforcing relationships between actions and attributes. The approach improves both zero-shot and linear-probing performance on three action-recognition benchmarks. Those results support using language-defined concepts as a training space for adapting image representations to video, alongside changes that let the backbone model temporal information.
neurips-2023-language-based-action-conce.tldr: Language-generated action concepts guide self-supervised adaptation of an image CLIP model to video, improving performance on three action-recognition benchmarks.

paragraphs: Step-by-step language-model explanations can look like transparent accounts of how an answer was reached. This paper tests whether those explanations acknowledge factors that influence predictions. It finds that chain-of-thought explanations can systematically omit such influences, making a plausible explanation an unreliable account of why a model chose its answer.

The researchers introduce biasing features into prompts, including arranging example answer options so the correct answer is always A. Models respond to these features without mentioning them in their explanations. When the bias favors an incorrect answer, the models frequently produce reasoning that rationalizes that answer instead of exposing the influence.

Tests with GPT-3.5 and Claude 1.0 on 13 BIG-Bench Hard tasks show accuracy drops of up to 36%. A social-bias task also elicits stereotype-consistent justifications that omit the bias's influence. The findings show that fluent reasoning can increase apparent transparency without faithfully explaining a prediction, motivating targeted improvements in explanation faithfulness or alternative approaches to transparency.
neurips-2023-language-models-don-t-alway.tldr: Chain-of-thought explanations can rationalize biased answers while failing to disclose prompt features that influenced the model's prediction.

paragraphs: Some classification tasks have transformations that should leave the answer unchanged. Building models that respect these invariances while remaining expressive can require substantial computation or memory. This paper explores whether allowing probabilistic guarantees for both invariance and approximation can reduce those resource demands.

The proposed models are Randomized Linear Classifiers. The authors give conditions on parameters and sample sizes under which these models can, with high probability, approximate any smooth function while preserving invariance to compact group transformations. Both the probability qualification and the specified transformation class are central to the result: the guarantees concern a defined mathematical setting.

Using this theory, the authors construct three classifiers for sets, graphs, and spherical data. They show how probabilistic invariance and universality can be achieved with fewer resources than deterministic neural networks and their invariant counterparts. Experiments demonstrate benefits on invariant tasks where deterministic invariant networks are known to struggle. The work makes randomness a deliberate design tool for balancing expressivity, invariance, and resource use.
neurips-2023-probabilistic-invariant-lea.tldr: Randomized Linear Classifiers use probabilistic approximation and invariance guarantees to reduce resources for classification on sets, graphs, and spherical data.

paragraphs: This paper treats replicability as a mathematical property of reinforcement learning algorithms. In discounted tabular decision processes with access to a generative model, a replicable algorithm should return exactly the same policy with high probability across independent datasets when its internal randomness is held fixed. Agreement concerns the policy itself, beyond similar performance.

The authors provide an efficient algorithm for near-optimal policy estimation with sample and time complexity scaling cubically in the number of state-action pairs, alongside other problem parameters. They also prove a lower bound with cubic dependence for deterministic algorithms. This establishes a computationally achievable guarantee and a restriction for that subclass.

Relaxing the requirement changes the tradeoffs. An efficient algorithm with total-variation indistinguishability uses quadratically scaling sample complexity; converting it to exact replicability preserves that sample complexity but incurs exponential running time. Requiring output policies only to be close under a statistical divergence yields linear scaling. These results distinguish the costs of exact agreement, distributional similarity, and approximate policy agreement.
neurips-2023-replicability-in-reinforcem.tldr: The paper formalizes replicability in reinforcement learning and shows how exact versus approximate policy agreement changes sample and computational costs.

paragraphs: Content recommendation platforms influence what creators produce through the rewards they offer. Because creators compete strategically, a reward rule also shapes the resulting content distribution and overall system welfare. This paper studies how platforms can design those incentives to guide competition toward desirable long-term outcomes.

The authors identify a fundamental limitation of a class called Merit-based Monotone Mechanisms. Within the studied framework, these mechanisms necessarily lose a constant fraction of the optimal welfare. The result concerns this particular class of reward rules and motivates looking beyond it when designing incentives for competing creators.

The proposed Backward Rewarding Mechanisms generate competition with a potential-game structure: creators' strategic behavior is directed toward optimizing a shared potential function. The authors show that this function can be designed to match any given welfare metric. They also describe a parameterization allowing direct welfare optimization within the feasible mechanism space when the metric is not explicitly defined. This connects reward design to the collective objective the platform wants creator competition to serve.
neurips-2023-rethinking-incentives-in-re.tldr: The paper proves a welfare limit for merit-based monotone rewards and proposes mechanisms that align creator competition with a chosen welfare objective.

paragraphs: Reducing a training dataset can save substantial computation, but incorrect labels make it harder to choose a useful subset. This paper studies pruning when training also includes relabeling methods that correct erroneous annotations. The selection problem becomes finding examples that best support accurate label correction across the original dataset.

The authors formalize this problem and show a proportional relationship between an example's probability of being correctly relabeled and prediction confidence in its neighborhood within the selected subset. Prune4Rel uses that relationship to select a subset maximizing total neighborhood confidence across all training examples. This links the pruning objective directly to relabeling accuracy and generalization.

Experiments cover four real noisy datasets and one synthetic noisy dataset. The authors report improvements over baselines of up to 9.1% with relabeling models and up to 21.6% with a standard model. These are the largest reported gains, rather than uniform improvements of those sizes. The results support choosing retained examples according to how well they help repair noisy supervision throughout the data.
neurips-2023-robust-data-pruning-under-l.tldr: Prune4Rel selects training subsets that maximize neighborhood confidence to support accurate label correction and improve learning with noisy annotations.

paragraphs: SafeDICE studies learning from existing demonstrations when avoiding unsafe behavior is a priority. The available data include demonstrations marked as non-preferred and demonstrations without such labels. The challenge is to learn a policy that imitates preferred behavior while excluding constraint-violating behavior, even though ordinary imitation learning encourages copying what the demonstrations contain.

The proposed hyperparameter-free algorithm works in the space of stationary distributions, which describe the patterns of behavior associated with a policy. It directly estimates distribution corrections for a policy that imitates the demonstrations after excluding non-preferred behavior. This gives the negative examples an active role in shaping what the learned policy should avoid.

In experiments, SafeDICE learns a safer policy than the baselines, satisfying the cost constraint without degrading reward performance. This is an empirical finding for the evaluated setting. The method's contribution is to make non-preferred demonstrations useful for offline imitation through distribution correction, connecting behavioral avoidance with learning from a fixed collection of demonstrations.
neurips-2023-safedice-offline-safe-imita.tldr: SafeDICE uses non-preferred demonstrations to learn safer offline imitation policies, meeting tested cost constraints without reducing reward performance.

paragraphs: Machine unlearning aims to remove requested data's influence from a trained model without starting training again. This paper examines a security concern within that process: data update requests can themselves be malicious. It studies whether an adversary can use the selective-forgetting interface to mount effective attacks.

The authors consider two ways requests can arrive. In the static setting, the adversary submits all malicious updates together. In the sequential setting, requests arrive over time. They formulate sequential attacks as a stochastic optimal control problem and develop optimization algorithms to find effective malicious requests in the studied settings.

The paper combines theoretical analyses with extensive experiments that validate the proposed attacks' effectiveness. Its contribution is to treat the handling of forgetting requests as a security-relevant part of the learning system. Distinguishing simultaneous from sequential requests also makes the timing of adversarial interaction explicit, broadening the study beyond a single batch of malicious updates.
neurips-2023-static-and-sequential-malic.tldr: The paper develops and analyzes attacks that exploit malicious data update requests during machine unlearning, both in batches and sequentially.

paragraphs: This paper analyzes linear regression when observations are dependent and a linear model need not exactly describe the data. It studies random-design regression under beta-mixing dependence and derives finite-sample upper bounds. Allowing misspecification matters because the analysis must accommodate errors beyond the strictly realizable martingale-noise setting.

The main result recovers, up to constant factors, the variance term predicted by the Central Limit Theorem. That term represents the problem's noise level. Matching it gives the bound a connection to the particular statistical instance, and the analysis degrades gracefully as misspecification is introduced into the regression problem.

The sharpness claim applies after a burn-in and in the moderate-deviations regime. Within that regime, the leading-order term is not inflated by mixing-time factors. These qualifications define where the result is strongest. The contribution is a more precise account of regression error with dependent data, showing that the leading noise term can retain the appropriate scale even without assuming that the linear model is exactly correct.
neurips-2023-the-noise-level-in-linear-r.tldr: The paper derives sharp regression bounds for dependent, potentially misspecified data that recover the appropriate leading noise term after a burn-in.

paragraphs: Training-data analysis has focused heavily on classification, leaving numerical prediction tasks less explored. TRIAGE addresses this gap with a framework for characterizing regression data across a broad class of regressors. It examines how individual examples behave during training so that dataset decisions can reflect the model's patterns of estimation.

The framework uses conformal predictive distributions to construct a model-agnostic TRIAGE score. Tracking this score through training allows examples to be characterized as underestimated, overestimated, or well estimated. This turns sample-level training dynamics into an organized description of the data, rather than relying only on an overall measure of predictive performance.

The authors show consistent characterization and demonstrate improved performance through data sculpting and filtering in multiple regression settings. They also use the framework beyond individual examples, for dataset selection and feature acquisition. These applications show how a common characterization method can support several data-related decisions, connecting the behavior of individual training samples with broader choices about what information a regression model learns from.
neurips-2023-triage-characterizing-and-a.tldr: TRIAGE scores regression examples throughout training to guide data filtering, dataset selection, and feature acquisition.

paragraphs: Neural activity and behavior vary across repeated trials of the same task. This paper aims to capture that joint variability in an interpretable model of a mouse sensory-motor pathway. It uses recordings from a tactile detection task in which the mouse reports detection by licking.

The model is a large recurrent spiking neural network fitted through gradient-based optimization. To handle variation between trials, the authors use optimal transport to define a distance between distributions of recorded and generated trials. This provides a training comparison that explicitly addresses the collection of different trial outcomes and their variability.

The method is applied to artificial data and recordings spanning six cortical areas. The fitted network generates realistic cortical activity and predicts jaw movements across the main modes of variation between trials. Analysis also identifies an unexpected mode associated with task-irrelevant mouse movements. These findings show the value of modeling trial distributions for connecting neural activity with behavior and uncovering variation beyond the task's intended response.
neurips-2023-trial-matching-capturing-va.tldr: Optimal-transport trial matching fits a spiking neural network that captures variability in mouse cortical activity and jaw movements.

paragraphs: The paper studies online convex optimization when decisions lie in an unbounded domain and the comparison sequence can change arbitrarily over time. No algorithm can achieve low regret against every possible comparison sequence simultaneously. The authors therefore seek guarantees that adapt to the sequence's complexity relative to available prior knowledge.

Their framework describes the comparison sequence using sparse coding over a user-chosen dictionary. The regret bound depends on the sequence's energy and how sparsely that dictionary represents it. This lets the choice of representation express prior knowledge and makes the guarantee sensitive to structure in the particular sequence being compared against.

With a wavelet dictionary, the resulting bound improves on prior work by depending on the magnitude of the sequence's average instead of its largest magnitude, and on deviations from that average instead of total uncentered magnitude. These changes capture different aspects of scale and variation. The proof also separates function approximation from regret minimization, simplifying the analysis while retaining flexibility in how sequence complexity is measured.
neurips-2023-unconstrained-dynamic-regre.tldr: Sparse coding yields adaptive regret bounds for unbounded online optimization by measuring changing comparison sequences through a user-chosen dictionary.

paragraphs: WildfireSpreadTS is a remote-sensing dataset for predicting wildfire spread at 24-hour intervals. It contains 13,607 images covering 607 United States fire events from January 2018 through October 2021. Each event includes a daily observation sequence, allowing researchers to study how a fire develops over time.

The inputs combine detected active fires with information about fuel, terrain, and weather across 23 channels. Active-fire maps have a spatial resolution of 375 meters. The time-series organization and additional input modalities distinguish the dataset from existing public resources described in the paper and support models that use multiple observations of a spreading fire.

The dataset presents several stated challenges: many input channels, temporal structure, highly imbalanced labels, and noisy fire detections affected by smoke, clouds, and detection inaccuracies. Complex physical processes add further difficulty. The release is intended to support research on temporal modeling, noise resistance, generative methods, uncertainty estimation, and optimization for many input dimensions; its contribution is the dataset and the research opportunities it enables.
neurips-2023-wildfirespreadts-a-dataset-.tldr: WildfireSpreadTS provides daily multimodal observations of 607 fire events to support 24-hour wildfire spread prediction.
